newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco pact gives bondholders case of the shakes.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco pact gives bondholders case of the shakes.

text.p: Tobacco bond prices fell on Monday as buying dried up on uncertainty about the implications of last Friday's news of a settlement between tobacco companies and the states, market players said.

News of the settlement broke late on Friday when the staff at most trading firms had already left for the day. As a result, most bond players had to wait until Monday morning to register their reaction.
On Monday, spreads of RJR Nabisco Holdings Inc bonds were quoted 15-20 basis points wider, while Philip Morris Cos bonds were quoted five basis points wider.
But traders pointed out actual trading of tobacco bonds was low, suggesting investor were mulling over the implications of the deal.
"We saw some weakeness because some of the guys who had positions didn't want to buy any more," said one trader.
The trader noted prices of tobacco company bonds had surged last week as investors bought in anticipation of the pact.
"We will have to wait to really see what happens. There is just so much to dig through, it's hard for people to figure out what they want to do," he added.
On Monday afternoon, Standard and Poor's acknowledged the uncertain implications of the settlement by leaving tobacco companies on CreditWatch with negative implications.
The ratings agency placed the debt of the major tobacco companies on negative CreditWatch on April 17, 1997.
"A major uncertainty is how much (each company) can cope with the settlement through price increases on tobacco products," said Nicholas Riccio, a S&P tobacco analyst.
"If you can't pass on the costs through price increases, you will have to borrow to pay the settlement," added Nicole Delz Lynch, another tobacco analyst at S&P.
Riccio said a final decision on ratings may not be made until Congress passes the necessary legislation to implement the accord.
He said that within the next two or three months, S&P hoped to issue a more extensive review of how the current settlement would impact each tobacco company.
Late on Monday, Moody's Investors Service affirmed its current ratings and negative outlooks for tobacco companies as well.
Analyst also expressed caution in their assessments.
Carol Levenson, an analyst with the publication, Gimmie Credit, said both RJR Nabisco and Philip Morris would be likely to survive the agreement in its current form.
She said this prediction assumed that neither company spun-off its non-tobacco division which will be needed to provide vital revenue to support the payments.
Based on preliminary estimates, the major tobacco companies would be able to finance their payments by raising cigarette prices and issuing additional debt, she said.
RJR Reynolds' rating would likely be downgraded to junk status from Baa3/BBB-minus in the near term if the agreement is approved because of its heavier borrowing requirments, she said .
Levenson said Philip Morris, currently rated A2/A, would eventually be downgraded to the BBB area.
She noted, however, "Although much of the financial uncertainty will be removed, it doesn't disappear entirely."
-Douglas Brown, U.S. Corporate Bond Unit, 212-859-1662
